video_title: Adam Posen Thinks Things Could Get 'Messy' for the Fed | Odd Lots
gist: Recorded at Jackson Hole right after Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's speech, Adam Posen grades it a B-minus, argues Warsh has effectively pre-committed the Fed to hiking (and that failing to hike would be read as political capitulation), and calls for fed funds 75-100bp higher within six months with inflation stuck in a 3.5-4.5% range. He also warns that the Mervyn King-led Fed communications task force is the sleeper source of radical change, and argues AI has begun boosting productivity in the last ~18 months while job displacement is still not visible in the data.

themes.theme: Warsh's Jackson Hole speech: a hike now baked in

insights.claim: Adam Posen grades the new Fed chair's Jackson Hole speech a B-minus by normal standards, but says it reads far better given the preceding months of confusion, and could be upgraded to a B-plus retroactively if it proves to be a pivot away from the chair's erratic early months.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: A grudging upgrade from a prominent critic signals the Fed chair's communication risk premium may be peaking rather than rising.
insights.quote: It's a B-minus speech.

insights.claim: Despite the chair's anti-forward-guidance stance, the fourth section of his speech laid out the full litany of reasons inflation will persist or rise, which functionally amounts to forward guidance that a tightening is coming even though he never said the concluding sentence.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Markets should price the speech as a de facto hiking commitment even though no explicit guidance was given.
insights.quote: for all the anti forward guidance he basically set up, they have to hike now

insights.claim: If the Fed does not hike after this speech, the failure will be widely interpreted either as capitulation to Trump or as the chair having gotten ahead of his committee, both of which damage credibility.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: A September/December hold is not a neutral outcome; it becomes a credibility event with duration and dollar consequences.
insights.quote: things could get really messy because if they don't hike, then people start saying was that because of Trump

insights.claim: The chair used the Jackson Hole appearance to nail down housekeeping that had been left ambiguous, explicitly confirming core PCE at 2% as the target.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Removes a live tail risk that the new regime would redefine or shift the inflation target.
insights.quote: core PC 2%. That's the target.

insights.claim: The chair signaled that wage inflation is not a good predictor of overall inflation, downgrading the labor-cost channel as a policy trigger.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Average hourly earnings and ECI prints should carry less weight in predicting this Fed's reaction function than under prior chairs.
insights.quote: He doesn't think wage inflation is a very good predictor of overall inflation

insights.claim: The chair also endorsed financial conditions as an important input to policy, a mainstream and defensible position that adds another channel through which market moves feed back into Fed decisions.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Easing financial conditions could itself provoke tightening, capping equity melt-ups.

insights.claim: The speech's long section on 'principles' was a strategic error that muddled the message, because principle statements either read as bromides or raise more questions than they answer, and were unnecessary for a chair who claims to dislike forward guidance.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Expect continued communication noise and headline risk around this chair's set-piece speeches.

insights.claim: The speech was 'hawk-ish' with a dash rather than hawkish: it established that inflation is going in the wrong direction and policy has been insufficiently restrictive, but stopped well short of the aggressive Powell-2022-style campaign posture.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: Argues for a short, shallow hiking sequence rather than a re-run of the 2022 rapid-tightening trade.
insights.quote: I found it to be hawk-ish, which is like with a dash between the hawk and the ish

insights.claim: Everything the chair said in the speech could have been said at the July meeting, at which he opted not to hike on the grounds he wanted more information, so the actual threshold for action remains undefined in an environment where shocks keep arriving.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: The 'wait for more data' framing can justify indefinite inaction, so hike-timing conviction should be discounted.

insights.claim: This Jackson Hole was deliberately staged as a normal, low-drama gathering by the chair and his team, in sharp contrast with the prior year that was dominated by attacks on the Fed, fears for independence, and a standing ovation for the outgoing chair.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: A de-escalation signal on Fed-institutional risk, at least at the level of stagecraft.

themes.theme: Maximal discretion and the chair's grip on the committee

insights.claim: The most worrying and most consistent thread across the new chair's confirmation hearings, first two press conferences, ECB Sintra remarks, and the Jackson Hole speech is an attempt to maximize last-minute discretion without pre-committing before any meeting.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Higher meeting-by-meeting event risk and wider rate-vol; option premia around FOMC dates should stay elevated.
insights.quote: trying to maximize his last minute discretion

insights.claim: The chair's language that inflation must head in the right direction 'at the right speed' is empty without a declared speed, because direction alone is exactly the framework that produced five years of above-target inflation.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Absence of a stated disinflation pace means the Fed retains room to tolerate 3-handle inflation indefinitely.

insights.claim: Pure discretion is a personality-dependent regime whose credibility dies with the individual, which is the 'Weekend at Bernie's problem' that made Greenspan-circa-1999 policy fragile and motivated the inflation-targeting and accountability push by Bernanke, Mishkin and Posen.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Personalized Fed credibility is a fat-tail risk: any shock to the chair becomes a shock to the whole policy anchor.

insights.claim: A maximal-discretion stance is especially odd for a chair who comes from the Hoover Institution, is seen as conservative, and was mentored by the late John Taylor, the standard-bearer for rules-based policy.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Ideological priors about a 'rules-based conservative' chair are a poor guide to how this Fed will actually behave.
insights.quote: it's really odd for somebody coming from the Hoover Institution who has been seen as a conservative who was mentored by the late John Taylor

insights.claim: The Fed chair's role is unspecified in the system and varies over time, but the Fed has given more power and deference to the chair than peers essentially since Volcker, in contrast with the ECB's consensus-driven design and the Bank of England's debate-first culture.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Reading the FOMC means reading the chair; other members' speeches carry less information than at the ECB or BoE.

insights.claim: Fed committee norms include an unwritten rule that only a limited number of members dissent at any one meeting and that the chair never loses a vote, a norm even Volcker respected by conceding rather than being outvoted.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Dissent counts are a weak signal of true committee division; the chair's stance is effectively the policy path.
insights.quote: there's sort of an informal rule only so many people dissent on the committee at any one meeting

insights.claim: Posen believes the new chair's stated welcome for a 'family fight' and more dissent is not sincere, though he concedes that if taken at face value the diagnosis is correct because debate had atrophied.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Do not expect genuinely contested FOMC votes; treat promised openness as messaging rather than a governance change.
insights.quote: I think Kevin Warsh is saying what you just said, Joe, that I am okay with more dissent and more debate. I don't believe him.

insights.claim: Low dissent under Powell was partly a deliberate and defensible choice to avoid signaling panic during Covid and disunity while the Fed was under overt political attack, but it built self-reinforcing momentum in which each meeting without a dissent raised the psychological bar for the next one.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Suppressed internal debate is a mechanism for persistent policy error, and one worth watching as a leading indicator of future misses.

insights.claim: Posen cites his Bank of England experience under Mervyn King, who allowed a free vote on QE and then asked for a moratorium on publicly relitigating whether QE works, as a legitimate crisis-time version of the same suppression of debate.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Central bank message discipline in crises is normal, which makes it harder to distinguish healthy solidarity from groupthink in real time.

themes.theme: Fed independence: where the real line sits

insights.claim: A certain amount of presidential yelling at or scapegoating the Fed is normal and was historically even healthy, functioning as public cover while officials privately signaled the Fed should do its job, under Volcker, Greenspan, Bernanke and Yellen alike.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Presidential criticism of the Fed is not by itself a tradeable independence signal; the escalation categories below are.
insights.quote: a certain amount of yelling at or scapegoating the fed is part of the game

insights.claim: The genuine economic red line for Fed independence is fiscal dominance: a Treasury secretary or president demanding the Fed help sell US bonds regardless of the inflation picture, which officials must answer by insisting long-run credibility is what actually sells the bonds.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Watch for Fed rhetoric shifting toward funding-cost or debt-service considerations as the tell for fiscal dominance, a long-end and inflation-breakeven trade.
insights.quote: Now I'm here to help you sell the bonds. You're preserving the long term credibility.

insights.claim: The unprecedented escalation under Trump was structural rather than rhetorical: threats to strip Reserve Bank presidents of their votes, to rapidly turn them over with political appointees instead of staggered terms, to change the Fed's mandate, and to pressure the Fed's budget.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Governance changes to voting rights and appointment terms, not tweets, are the events that would repricing US inflation risk premia.
insights.quote: They were threatening to take away the votes of some of the reserve Bank presidents or quickly turn over the reserve Bank presidents

insights.claim: Posen characterizes the use of legal action against individual Fed governors, naming Governor Cook, as outrageous and arguably criminal, distinguishing it sharply from ordinary political carping.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Litigation against sitting governors is the visible edge of an attempt to change the committee's composition by force.

insights.claim: Posen frames politicizing appointments and removals as 'almost as big' a threat as fiscal dominance precisely because it is the means to achieve fiscal dominance.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Personnel moves are the leading indicator; the funding-cost capture would be the lagging, priced consequence.

themes.theme: The communications task force as the sleeper radical

insights.claim: Attention is concentrated on the balance sheet committee, but Posen expects that one to produce sober, practical, smaller-scale recommendations than people anticipate, while the communications committee is where the genuinely radical surprise will come from.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Positioning for balance-sheet drama may be mispriced; the tail risk is a shock to the Fed's information output instead.
insights.quote: I think the communications committee is probably where we're going to get the biggest surprise.

insights.claim: The communications task force is chaired by Mervyn King with Peter Fisher and members including Raghuram Rajan, Jeremy Stein and Karen Dynan, and both King and Fisher have publicly turned sharply skeptical of central bank communication in recent years.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: The membership is stacked toward cutting back Fed forecasts and guidance; anyone whose process depends on the SEP or dot plot faces regime risk.
insights.quote: I think this is the committee that has the biggest chance of a surprise to being radical.

insights.claim: Mervyn King's arc is the striking irony: as Bank of England chief economist he pioneered UK inflation targeting after sterling's 1992 ERM exit and fathered the fan charts as a transparency and accountability device, but since retiring he argues central banks cannot forecast and therefore should not be publishing all this information.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: The intellectual architect of transparency now leading the review is the strongest signal that Fed disclosure will be reduced, not expanded.

insights.claim: The King/Fisher view holds that markets have become too dependent on central bank information, generating moral hazard and mispriced risk, and that yields and yield volatility should be higher than they have been so markets take risk seriously, produce more informative pricing, and generate fewer bubbles.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: An explicit policy preference for higher rate volatility is a direct argument for owning convexity and against short-vol carry strategies.
insights.quote: yields and volatility around yields should be higher than it had been

insights.claim: Posen believes the chair's true instincts remain that the Fed cannot forecast, the market knows more than the Fed on many things, and spoon-feeding markets creates moral hazard, even though the Jackson Hole speech softened the more extreme statements with a 'hall of mirrors' acknowledgment that the market is not always right.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Expect less guidance, fewer forecasts and more market-driven price discovery, with rate vol structurally higher than the post-GFC norm.

insights.claim: The prior 'play the ball, not the referee' message was, in Posen's telling, the single most annoying thing this chair said to the central banking community, because it effectively told markets they set the path.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Its walk-back reduces the risk of a self-referential loop where market pricing dictates policy.
insights.quote: of all the things that annoyed central banking community, that may have been the most annoying

themes.theme: Inflation call and the rate path

insights.claim: Posen expects the Fed to hike in September, and if not September then certainly December, with fed funds 75 to 100 basis points higher than current levels six months out.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated, size-specific rate call to trade against the front end and SOFR strip.
insights.quote: And so six months from now fed funds will be 75 pips or 100 pips higher than it is now.

insights.claim: Inflation may tick down a tenth or two over the next couple of months on energy, but will stay in a 3.5% to 4.5% range with upside risk until the Fed tightens meaningfully.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Explicit range call: fading disinflation trades on one or two soft prints is the wrong reflex.
insights.quote: we're going to be in this three and a half to four and a half range with some upside risk

insights.claim: The persistence is in core services rather than imported goods, and three-, six- and twelve-month moving averages are in the high threes and rising, meaning the inflation problem is domestic and momentum-driven rather than tariff mechanics.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Domestic services persistence is the kind the Fed must break with demand destruction, arguing for higher-for-longer real rates.

insights.claim: Posen's earlier call with Peter Orszag of Lazard for 4% PCE inflation rested on the labor market being more resilient than the Fed thought, credit being more available, financial conditions being less tight than assumed, looser fiscal policy, and inflation momentum built up over roughly 55-64 months above target; CPI subsequently exceeded 4% earlier in the year.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: The forecast framework already scored a hit, raising the weight investors should give its current 3.5-4.5% extension.

insights.claim: The core prediction was not about any specific shock but about fragility: the system was primed so that whatever the next inflation shock turned out to be it would land harder, and the actual trigger, the bombing of Iran and Strait of Hormuz disruption, was unforecastable.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Trade the fragility, not the shock: with anchors weak, buy cheap inflation-shock convexity rather than trying to time geopolitics.
insights.quote: But I knew there was going to be an inflation shock, and we were primed to have more.

insights.claim: Posen argues Powell's Fed was late hiking in 2022, profoundly mistaken to cut multiple times last year, and is behind the curve again now, a critique he considers legitimate even though the tone of the pre-appointment attacks on the prior regime was unnecessary.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: If the Fed is behind the curve again, terminal rate pricing is too low and the curve too steeply cutting.
insights.quote: was late to the game and hiking in 2022 was early

insights.claim: The international comparison does not flatter the Fed: once you control for imported energy dependence, inherited inflation, and fiscal looseness, the ECB and Swiss National Bank kept inflation down while the Bank of England is roughly level with the Fed, making the Fed more of an outlier.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Undercuts the 'inflation was global, nobody could have done better' defense and supports a structural US inflation premium versus Europe.
insights.quote: So the ECB has kept inflation down. The Swiss National Bank skipped inflation relatively down, Bank of England almost the same as the fed.

insights.claim: Part of the US inflation excess is fiscal: a Biden fiscal blowout on entering office that probably was not necessary, no subsequent consolidation, and then Trump's first-year long-term tax cuts.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Persistent fiscal impulse means the Fed must run tighter than otherwise, supporting higher real yields.
insights.quote: because Biden did do a fiscal blowout on coming into office. That probably wasn't necessary. And then there's been no consolidation.

insights.claim: If you take the chair's own claim that inflation is ultimately the Fed's responsibility seriously, then fiscal laxity becomes an additional reason for the Fed to hike rather than an excuse for the inflation overshoot.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: A hawkish inversion of the usual fiscal-dominance argument: loose fiscal should raise, not lower, the expected policy rate.
insights.quote: all this fiscal laxity in discipline should be another reason to hike

insights.claim: The Fed staff's repeated drumbeat that the labor market could collapse was contradicted in real time by outside economists including Posen, Michael Strain and Diane Swonk, and the labor market did not collapse, which is a concrete instance of the Fed getting a forecast wrong for identifiable reasons.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Fed labor-market pessimism has a poor recent track record; fade dovish pivots that rest on projected labor weakness.

insights.claim: Tariffs and anti-immigration policy hit inflation with a J-curve lag because businesses and people need time to make and implement decisions, which is why the inflationary effects showed up later than critics expected.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Policy-shock inflation is back-loaded; the absence of an immediate print is not evidence the effect is absent.

themes.theme: AI labor market and productivity: no displacement yet

insights.claim: There is much more indicative evidence of an AI-driven improvement in productivity than of any effect on the labor market, and hiring data including for coders shows job growth continuing in exactly the industries thought most exposed.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: The 'AI is destroying jobs' narrative is not yet visible in the data; positioning on labor-displacement themes is running ahead of evidence.
insights.quote: we're just not seeing, job growth continues in those industries

insights.claim: If AI job displacement is coming, it is currently showing up only as reduced hiring of younger workers rather than as job losses.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Watch entry-level and youth hiring rates as the earliest AI-displacement indicator, not headline unemployment.
insights.quote: If it is coming, it is showing up in the lack of hiring of younger people.

insights.claim: Posen cautions against attributing weak hiring entirely to AI, because much of it is overhang from the enormous post-Covid reshuffling and redefinition of jobs during reemployment, a point the Fed chair also made in his speech.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Conflating post-Covid normalization with AI displacement leads to systematically wrong macro conclusions.

insights.claim: The J-curve explanation for missing displacement is that there is an efficient period, probably under ten years and likely closer to five, in which humans and AI work together while businesses restructure and specialized applications and robotics get built, and during that window few jobs are lost.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Gives a rough five-year clock on the transition, useful for sizing the duration of labor-market complacency.
insights.quote: Brynjolfsson has spoken about a J curve

insights.claim: The 'messy jobs' thesis from LSE researchers argues that almost every job, including long haul trucking, carries far more specific knowledge, relationships and complementarity than exposure studies assume, making consulting-firm and international-institution 'most exposed sectors' rankings probably misleading.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Sector 'AI exposure' screens used to short labor-intensive businesses are likely a poor basis for positioning.

insights.claim: The Industrial Revolution analogy cuts against exposure studies: 19th-century English skilled weavers genuinely were replaced by automated weaving, but outside that very narrow job description the actual displacement pattern looked nothing like what an ex-ante study would have predicted.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Historical base rates argue that displacement will be concentrated and idiosyncratic rather than broad and predictable.

insights.claim: At an off-the-record meeting a very senior figure from the AI community, asked by a well-known academic economist why the predicted job apocalypse had not materialized, answered that people turn out to really like dealing with humans and do not always want to deal with machines.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Even AI insiders are privately conceding a demand-side human preference constraint that most displacement models ignore.
insights.quote: it turns out people really like dealing with humans and don't always want to deal with machines

insights.claim: Posen dates the AI productivity boost to growth as only kicking in within roughly the last year and a half, and places himself just on the pessimistic side of the debate about how much of measured productivity growth is attributable to AI.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: A recent, modest start to AI productivity gains argues against models that already assume a step-change in trend growth.
insights.quote: the AI productivity boost to growth kicked in until very recently

insights.claim: The big productivity and disinflation gains come far down the chain, not at the chip-making stage: chipmakers like Intel and Texas Instruments following Moore's Law in the 1990s showed up only modestly in GDP, while the real gains arrived when McDonald's, Walmart and UPS transformed their businesses around the technology.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: The AI productivity trade eventually rotates from semiconductor suppliers to adopting incumbents in retail, food and logistics.
insights.quote: But the gains really happened when McDonald's and Walmart and UPS and everybody transformed their businesses to take advantage of it.

insights.claim: Consumer-facing AI use, such as having a model book the cheapest flight with seat preferences, generates real utility and time savings that largely do not show up in GDP, which is why measured productivity lags the perceived usefulness of the technology.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: A structural wedge between AI's felt usefulness and measured output justifies skepticism of near-term GDP-based AI bull cases.

insights.claim: Tracy Alloway's shed-roofing anecdote illustrates the limits of AI substitution for trades: ChatGPT and YouTube recommended an adhesive shingle product that only worked above 60 degrees Fahrenheit and neither source registered that the job was in New England rather than Florida.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: Context-blindness in current models is a concrete reason physical-trades labor demand holds up longer than exposure models imply.
insights.quote: we realized that that product only worked in environments that were above 60

themes.theme: GDP measurement and the Nvidia question

insights.claim: A report suggesting roughly 0.3% of GDP was being missed in the accounting for chips designed in the US but manufactured in Taiwan matters not for the Fed, which does not target GDP, but for assessing whether AI has actually produced a productivity transformation.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: A recurring annual 0.3% attributable to AI would materially change the productivity narrative even though it does not change policy directly.
insights.quote: If this 0.3% say, a year was overlooked and it is directly attributable to the AI sector, then that tells a different story about productivity.

insights.claim: The two measurement issues are the old value-added problem of allocating output between domestic and foreign production in complex supply chains, and the recurring claim in every technological revolution that GDP fails to capture true value, which economists answer with market value and hedonic quality adjustment.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Statistical revisions to AI-era output are more likely to be reallocations than genuine upgrades to the growth path.

insights.claim: None of the GDP allocation debate changes the economic substance for Nvidia: the bottom line does not move, the money still flows to shareholders, investment and workers, and US-based chip designers are still getting paid.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal and Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Statistical-measurement headlines about AI GDP are not a signal for equity positioning in the affected companies.

insights.claim: The current wave of social scientists leaving universities and think tanks for AI companies has precedent in the internet boom, when Hal Varian became Google's first chief economist, but is an order of magnitude larger and driven by money, prestige and the belief in being part of changing the world.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: A structural shift in where economic policy expertise sits, which affects whose analysis regulators and markets end up hearing.

insights.claim: The key difference from the Google/Amazon era is that AI labs are hiring economists explicitly to shape policy for the AI transition rather than to build internal pricing and auction tools, which makes their public claims about job creation and regulation inherently discountable even when sincerely held.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Treat in-house AI-lab economic research on jobs and regulation as advocacy-adjacent; weight independent think tank and academic work more heavily.

insights.claim: Beyond compensation, joining an AI company costs an economist independence of voice and of research agenda, because these remain companies with hierarchies, and Posen says a noted techno-optimist academic turned down every offer for exactly that reason.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: The credibility discount on in-house AI economics is a durable feature, creating value in genuinely independent research.
insights.quote: You're losing your independent voice, what you choose to work on.

themes.theme: Powell's legacy and the asymmetry of central bank reputations

insights.claim: Central bank reputations are asymmetric: Arthur Burns is remembered as the bad tenure for inflation while Bernanke is remembered fondly despite presiding over a financial crisis and years of high unemployment, implying Powell's 64-65 months of above-target inflation will weigh heavily on how his tenure ages.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: If reputational risk is skewed toward inflation, incoming and sitting Fed officials are structurally biased toward hawkishness.

insights.claim: Three of the four predecessor Fed chairs, Greenspan, Yellen and Powell, had major stumbles in an early press conference, so the current chair's July press conference mess may prove to be growing pains rather than a signal about his policy framework.
insights.speaker: Adam Posen
insights.so_what: Base rates argue against extrapolating a new chair's early communication errors into a durable policy read.
